B2

How we searched

621 searches · 17 databases and search engines · English and Thai (199 searches with Thai-language queries) · 7 November 2026 [D05.stamp]

What counts as one search. One query of words, names or field filters, run against a database, index, catalogue, portal, site search or web search engine, that got an answer, even with 0 hits. Not counted: 299 lookups of known items, 26 failed attempts (blocked, rate-limited, timed out, CAPTCHA or bot check), 22 checks inside documents already in hand, 4 attempts not run. Every interface of one database counts once. The full log has 972 rows. [D05.stamp]

What we looked for and did not find. Our four main absence claims (norms, regional languages, validations outside Bangkok, a fluency pass mark) were each attacked by two separate disproof checks that tried to prove them wrong; two were refuted and reworded. We say "we found none". The counts below are logged rows tied to each claim (searches, lookups and checks), so they do not add up to the 621 searches of the stamp, which count searches only.

The MoCA or MoCA-B in a regional language (Isan, Northern Thai, Southern Thai, Patani Malay), or results by home languageWe found none. Not refuted.172about 1584[D05.regional]
MoCA validations outside the Bangkok regionFirst wording refuted. Accuracy studies only in Khon Kaen [T06] and Chiang Mai (people with HIV; site from the authors' affiliations) [T14, T14.site]; reliability and concurrent validity in Chiang Mai adults with depression [T27]; the 2021 validation also recruited in Prachin Buri and Ang Thong [T02.sites]. None found in the South; no MoCA-B validation outside Bangkok.102about 1319[D05.outside_bkk]

Closest things we found (not what we looked for)

  • Norms: score bands from a four-region survey [T29.distribution]; shares flagged by age band in Chiang Mai city [T41.pinyopornpanish]; education effects in 93 healthy Bangkok volunteers, a conference abstract [T28.sample]; Mini MoCA means by age and schooling [T05.byage_edu]; Thai norms for other tests (TMSE, HIV test batteries, category fluency) [T41.tmse2015, T41.batteries, T41.fluency]; the developer's normative list has no Thai study [T40.norms].
  • Regional languages: Khon Kaen excluded people who could not speak Thai [T06.language]; an Udon Thani study admitted local-language speakers but used the unchanged Thai MoCA [T42.songtin]; a Narathiwat word set for the Mini-Cog (a different test) [T42.waheng]; Northern Thai versions of other tools [T42.pothirat, T42.kawilapat]; the developer offers regional versions for other countries, only standard Thai for Thailand [T40.menus].
  • The South: the MoCA is used there (for example after a positive AMT in Nakhon Si Thammarat [T35.moca]), and a Thai review of 12 MCI surveys found none from the South [T30.regions].

What we could not search. Scopus and Web of Science (no access); Google Scholar for Thai evidence (bot check); the Khon Kaen and Chulalongkorn university repositories (blocked); print abstract books; most grey literature and theses. [D05 caveat]

2020 national dementia guideline [T23.firstline, T23.secondline, T23.interp]First-line screen for suspected dementia: TMSE or MoCA. Second line: MoCA-B (below grade 4 or cannot read), RUDAS, MTMSE, IQCODE. MoCA: +1 for grade 6 or lower; flagged at or below 24.

B4

Reliability

Which type matters for this tool (our reasoning): a hand-scored screen that people repeat needs test-retest and inter-rater reliability first; internal consistency (alpha) matters less in a test that mixes abilities on purpose.

VersionTest-retestInter-raterInternal consistency

Total-score inter-rater agreement in other countries [F07]: Changsha r 0.926, n 53 [F07.tu2013] · Hong Kong alternate forms ICC 0.99 and 0.87, n 20 [F07.wong2018] · Amharic ICC 0.96, n 20 [F07.daniel2022] · Italian ICC 0.999, n 77 [F07.pirani2022] · Parkinson's ICC 0.81 [F07.gill2008] · Filipino 0.887, n 25 [F07.dominguez2013] · Cantonese ICC 0.96 [F07.chu2014]. Range about 0.80 to 0.999; samples small, designs differ, and two of the highest figures have the developer as co-author [F07.range, F07 caveat].

Scoring single items: the drawings · Stroke trial, 1,119 score sheets re-scored blind [F08.design]: trail-making 97% agreement (κ 0.94), cube 90% (0.80), clock contour 92% (0.49), clock numbers 89% (0.67), clock hands 72% (0.46); the re-scorer was stricter [F08.agreement, F08.direction] · Novice raters, clock: ICC 0.28 to 0.58 by set [F09.icc] · Developer's digital MoCA, original instructions: cube 0.58, clock numbers 0.50, clock hands 0.58 [F10.items].

Scores over time · Irish community adults, n 130, 2–4 months apart: ICC 0.81; standard error of measurement 1.5; a change must reach about 4 points to be trusted [F11.design, F11.results] · Developer's unpublished clinic observations: re-test differences of 3–4 points in at least 20% of patients [F06.letter2019] · Three Thai alternate forms, 8.1 to 8.3, "to decrease possible learning effects" [T40.versions].

Training, certification and who may give the test · Vendor claim, unpublished: 33% proficient before certification, 79% after one training [F06.proficiency] · The author's 2019 letter: his team had not conducted a study showing that training improves assessments [F06.letter2019] · We found no peer-reviewed study [D05.training] · New Zealand audit: 23% of junior doctors had ever had formal teaching; one session improved scoring [F12.audit, F12.teaching] · Since December 2025 certification is optional for total-score screening and still required to interpret sub-scores [F06.optional2025] · Free for publicly operated healthcare institutions, students and academic researchers [F06.free] · Clinical use without permission; free of charge to patients [F06.use] · Any clinician may give it; a health professional with cognitive expertise interprets it [F06.interpret] · Thai manuals: staff "trained and practised" in the tools; no mention of the developer's certification [T24.who, D05.cert_thai]. Vendor pages: checked 7 Nov 2026.

B5

What a positive screen means: PPV and NPV

Our illustration. Sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.80 (the pooled best at flagged at or below 24 was 80.48% / 81.19% [F04.moca_best]; the 2009 Thai poster version gave 0.80 / 0.80 [T01.poster_amci]). Base rates: 28% (the Khon Kaen clinic sample [T06.sample]); 20% and 10% are assumptions, close to a US guideline's estimates of 10.1% at ages 70–74 and 14.8%–25.2% at 75–84 [F17.prevalence]. [D01.inputs]

Formula [D01.formula]
PPV = sens × p ÷ (sens × p + (1 − spec) × (1 − p))
NPV = spec × (1 − p) ÷ (spec × (1 − p) + (1 − sens) × p)
p = share of the people screened who have MCI.

Base ratePPV: share of positives that are rightNPV: share of negatives that are rightKey
28% (Khon Kaen clinic)0.6087, about 6 in 100.9114[D01.p28]
20% (assumed)0.5, 1 in 20.9412[D01.p20]
10% (assumed)0.3077, about 3 in 100.973[D01.p10]

100 people at 10% [D01.icons]: 8 caught + 2 missed (the people with MCI) · 18 false alarms + 72 correctly cleared (everyone else). Positives: 8 true out of 8 + 18. A positive means "look closer", not "has MCI".

Other input pairs · The 2009 published abstract's 0.70 / 0.95 [T01.pub_cutoff]: PPV 0.8448 / 0.7778 / 0.6087 at 28% / 20% / 10% [D01.alt_published] · The meta-analysis's exact 0.8048 / 0.8119: PPV 0.6246 / 0.5168 / 0.3222 [D01.alt_meta].

Formula check · Khon Kaen's own 0.762 / 0.713 at 28% gives PPV 0.508 and NPV 0.8851, as printed (50.8%, 88.5%) [D01.t06check].

Printed predictive values depend on the sample · Montreal 2005: PPV 89%, NPV 91% for MCI, in samples where about half had the condition [F01.ppvnpv; F01 caveat] · MoCA-B 2015: PPV 85%, NPV 82%, accuracy 84% [T04.ppvnpv]; our reconstruction: 34 caught, 8 missed, 37 cleared, 6 false alarms [T04.recon].

Cochrane's worked example (dementia, not MCI) [F02.example] · 1,000 people, 6.5% with dementia: 65 cases, 1 missed, 449 false positives: about 7 work-ups per case found · Memory clinic, 50% with dementia: 30 missed, 250 false positives.

Cut-offs by schooling exist elsewhere · China (as Cochrane reports): flagged at or below 13 with no formal education, 19 with 1–6 years, 24 with 7 or more years (printed "13/14", "19/20", "24/25") [F02.lu_education] · Thai MoCA-Thai: we found none worked out by schooling [D05.edu_cutoff].

The Thai education point is worded in at least five ways [T39.educ_variants]: none (2009 abstract) · +1 for 6 years or fewer (2009 blog; T09; T11; T13; T33) · +1 below primary grade 6 (T32) · +1 for grade 6 or lower (T23) · +1 for less than grade 6 (T24). B7

MoCA vs MoCA-B: what changed, in words

How each version was built

  • MoCA (Montreal). From one author's clinical intuition (Z. Nasreddine): 10 domains, changed over 5 years of clinic use; 8 domains in the final version [F01.origin]. Pilot: 46 memory-clinic patients vs 46 healthy controls; 5 weak items replaced; scoring re-weighted [F01.pilot]. Validation 2005: 277 people (90 controls, 94 MCI, 93 mild AD) from two Montreal-area memory clinics, in English or French; controls aged 72.84 with 13.33 years of school [F01.sample, F01.sites, F01.languages]. First-version year: the developer's sources say 1996 or 1992; the paper gives none [F01.firstyear].
  • MoCA-Thai. Translated by Dr Solaphat Hemrungrojn, Chulalongkorn [T39.translator]; on the developer's site by May 2007 [T39.online2007]. The only account of the method: a linguist back-translated it, and 2 psychiatrists and 1 neurologist checked the content (co-author's blog, 2011) [T39.blog]; we found no published description [D05.translation]. Adapted: letter fluency with ก instead of F [T07.letter]; the Place item asks for the hospital's name [T03.place_item]; some memory words are familiar Thai substitutes (words never shown) [T39.memorywords]. Validated in 2009 conference abstracts [T01] and a 2021 paper from three hospitals [T02.sites]. Today: three Thai forms, 8.1 to 8.3 [T40.versions]; one form in April 2015 [T39.single2015].
  • MoCA-B. A joint project of the MoCA Clinic and Institute (Canada) and the Prince Mahidol Award Foundation and Faculty of Medicine, Chulalongkorn University (Thailand) [T04.developers]; unpublished French pilot, 10 intact vs 17 impaired with 12 years of school or less [T04.pilot]; validated in Bangkok, 2015: 85 people aged 55–80 with under 5 years of school [T04.sample].
  • Mini MoCA-Thai. A separate 15-point short form, about 5 minutes, by telephone; Siriraj, 2026 [T05.shortform].

What the MoCA-B changed [T04.changes, T04.cubeclock, T04.structure, T04.adjust]

AbilityMoCA: points [F01.points; T03.scoring]MoCA-B: points [T04.structure]Why the MoCA-B changed it
Visuospatialcube copy 1; clock drawing 3superimposed-objects recognition 3cube and clock depend heavily on schooling (planning, construction, 3-D perception)
Trail taskletters and numbers, 1numbers and dots, 1letters need literacy
Fluencyletter fluency, 1 (ก in Thai)fruit fluency, 2letter fluency needs literacy
Abstractiontwo-item verbal abstraction, 2word similarity with easier pairs, 3lower level of abstraction
Calculationserial subtraction, 3daily-life problem-solving, 3replaces serial 7s
Attentiondigits forward and backward 2; tapping 1modified digit Stroop, 3literacy-independent
Namingthree animals, 3animal naming with more detail, 4literacy affects recognition
Repetitiontwo sentences, 2not in the MoCA-B's structure—
Delayed recallfive words, 5five words, 5same
Orientation66same
Education points+1 for 12 years or less (Montreal) [F01.educ]; Thai guideline: +1 for grade 6 or lower [T23.interp]+1 for under 4 years, +1 more for people who cannot read or write fluently (paper) [T04.adjust]; Thai guideline: +1 for grade 4 or lower [T23.interp]after the paper's points, schooling no longer predicted the score [T04.adjust]
Timeabout 10 minutes [F01.format]15 to 21 minutes [T04.time]

What the Thai data say about single items

  • Naming: the Naming section is unreliable, α 0.593 [T03.seven_domain]; healthy controls scored 3.0 of 3 and naming dropped only in AD [T03.naming_scores]; Lion loaded .637, under the 0.65 bar; the Thai team: "too easy" [T03.loadings, T03.why_low]. Elsewhere, the Filipino version replaced one naming animal with one locals recognise [F05.adaptations].
  • Other weak items [T03.loadings, T03.why_low]: Clock Circle .486 and Digit Forward .607 ("too easy"); Repeat 2nd Sentence .527 and Place .568 ("too difficult"; Place = naming the hospital).
  • Orientation: Month and Year worked well; Date, Day and Place were too hard for elders who stay home (the authors' reading, not tested) [T03.month_year]. In community records with a different test (the AMT), dates were often missed, and the authors point to the Buddhist Era, lunar months and the twelve-year animal cycle [T19.dateitems, T19.calendar].
  • Fluency: the Thai point needs 11 or more ก words [T38.t08]; healthy Thai elders averaged 10.1 words (Thai ACE task) and 7.5 with 6 years of school or fewer [T07.means, T07.byeducation]; we found no Thai study that tested whether 11 is right [D05.fluency]; Thai words are hard to count by machine (split words, tone confusions) [T08.wordsplit].
  • Cube and clock: schooling changes them even in healthy Bangkok volunteers [T28.findings]; scorers disagree most on clock hands [F08.agreement].
B8

Statistics glossary

TermPlain meaningOur example
ReliabilityDoes the test give consistent scores?
Test-retest reliabilitySame people, same test, two occasions: do scores agree?r 0.92, n 26 [F01.retest]
Inter-rater reliabilityTwo scorers, same answers: do they agree?clock hands κ 0.46 [F08.agreement]
Internal consistency (Cronbach's α)Do the items agree with each other on one occasion?α 0.83 [F01.alpha]
Pearson rHow closely two sets of scores rise together (−1 to 1)MoCA vs MMSE r 0.87 [F01.mmse_r]
Spearman ρThe same idea, using ranksRUDAS-Thai ρ 0.6 [T06.spearman]
ICC (intraclass correlation)Agreement, not just correlation: also counts a whole-group shiftMoCA-B retest ICC 0.91 [T04.retest]
Kappa (κ)Agreement on categories beyond chanceThai κ 0.994, no n [T03.mocathai_rel]
CCC (concordance correlation)How close pairs of scores fall to "exactly equal"tablet vs paper 0.47 [T09.ccc]
Limits of agreement (Bland–Altman)The range that holds most person-by-person differences−7.63 to 4.98 points [T09.loa]
Minimum detectable changeSmallest change bigger than measurement errorabout 4 points [F11.results]
SensitivityOf people who have the condition, the share the test flags90% [F01.sens]
SpecificityOf people who don't, the share the test clears87% [F01.spec]
PPV / NPVOf positives / negatives, the share that are right; they depend on how common the condition isPPV about 3 in 10 at 10% [D01.p10]
AUC (area under the ROC curve)Pick one person with the condition and one without: how often the first scores worse (0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect). Not "% accurate".0.813: about 81 times in 100 [D03.meaning]
Youden indexSensitivity + specificity − 1; used to pick a "best" cut-offKhon Kaen's flagged at or below 19 [T06.cutoff19]
Likelihood ratio (LR+)How much a positive result raises the odds2.65 [T06.cutoff19]
Cut-offOur convention: "flagged at or below X"[D04.convention]
Criterion validityAgreement with a clinical diagnosisAUC 0.813 [T02.auc_hc]
Concurrent validityCorrelation with another test given at the same timeMMSE r 0.87 [F01.mmse_r]
Known-groups validityGroups that should differ do differ26.3 vs 21.3 [T04.means]
Construct validityThe score's structure fits the ability it claims to measureone general factor [T03.seven_domain]
Content validityThe items cover the skills they should; Montreal used this label for the MMSE correlation (our critique)[F01.contentvalidity]
PLS loadingHow strongly an item follows its factor; here above 0.65 counts as adequateLion .637 [T03.loadings]
AVE, composite reliability, rho AReliability indices from the factor model0.551, 0.895, 0.870 [T03.seven_domain]
Case-control ("two-gate") designDiagnosed patients vs separately recruited healthy people: makes accuracy look better[F05.rigour; F02.casecontrol]
Single-group designTest one group of people as they come, then diagnoseKhon Kaen [T06.sample]
Spectrum biasAccuracy distorted when the sample's range differs from real use[F02.casecontrol; F02.original]
Base rateShare with the condition among the people tested28% in Khon Kaen [T06.sample]
MCI / aMCIMild cognitive impairment: memory complaint, measurable loss, daily life intact, no dementia; amnestic = memory-led[F01.criteria]
NormsReference scores from healthy people, by age, schooling and so onSingapore, 1,103 adults [F14.sample]
QUADAS-2A checklist for bias in accuracy studies[F02.quality]
B9

Design of a Thai norms study (our proposal)

Why · We found no Thai MoCA norms by age, education or region [D05.norms]. The MoCA uses one rule plus one point; the MMSE-Thai 2002 has cut-offs by schooling [T41.mmse]. Community surveys at the Thai rule flagged 80.6% to 95.4% [T32.flagged, T33.flagged, T31.flagged]. Age and schooling drive scores: Spain, −0.19 points per year of age and +1.28 per year of education [F15.regression]; Singapore, age and education explain most of what the model explained [F14.effects]. Experts across Southeast Asia call for national norms [F16.norms].

Who Thai older people are (national survey, 2024) [T20]

Aged 60+14,027,411 people [T20.n60]
Age60–69: 59.3% · 70–79: 29.8% · 80+: 10.9% [T20.agegroups]
Schooling completednone 6.3% · below primary 60.9% · primary 12.6% · above primary 20.1% [T20.edulevels, T20.abovepri]; about 4 in 5 (79.9%) no schooling above primary (our arithmetic) [D02.calc]
RegionNortheast 30.1% · Central 26.9% · North 20.8% · South 11.8% · Bangkok 10.4% [T20.region]
No schooling above primary, by region (our arithmetic)Northeast 89.7% · North 86.4% · South 79.5% · Central 75.6% · Bangkok 48.9% [D02.areas]
Areaoutside municipal areas 57.1% [T20.nonmuni]
Literacy (any language)89.6%; 71.7% at 80+ [T20.literacy]

Our design

1. Sample. A random household sample of older adults in all five regions, the South included, stratified by age band, schooling, literacy, sex, municipal area and home language (Thai, Isan, Northern Thai, Southern Thai, Patani Malay). At least as large as Singapore's 1,103 healthy adults [F14.sample]; a 3,021-person, 14-province MoCA survey shows the fieldwork is possible [T29.sample].
2. Who counts as healthy. A clinician, blind to the MoCA, rules out dementia and MCI (CDR or DSM-5), unlike surveys that used the score alone [T18.definition; D05.community].
3. Testing. One current Thai form; trained raters; drawing items scored twice on a subsample [F08.agreement]; a retest subsample at about one month [F11.results].
4. Language. Give the test in Thai and record home language; where needed, build and check a regional-language version, as was done for a Northern Thai depression scale [T42.kawilapat; D05.regional].
5. Analysis. Regression-based norms by age, schooling, literacy and region, as in Singapore [F14.sample]; report means, spread and percentiles for each group.
6. Then validate. In a single-group community sample with clinical diagnosis, set cut-offs by schooling [D05.edu_cutoff], as China did (flagged at or below 13, 19 and 24, by schooling) [F02.lu_education].
7. Test the items on the way. The 11-word ก mark [D05.fluency; T07.means]; new naming pictures [T03.naming_scores]; orientation items [T03.month_year].

Our design, not a tested protocol.

B10

Limits of our own review

  • Depth. Of our 68 facts, 37 were checked against the full paper, 19 at abstract level only, 7 rest on secondary sources (conference abstracts, vendor pages, reports by other papers) and 5 are our own arithmetic [meta.counts]. The 2021 Thai validation was read only at abstract level [T02.adequate]: its reliability design and translation method are unknown to us.
  • Reach. We could not search Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar for Thai evidence, or the Khon Kaen and Chulalongkorn university repositories; grey literature and theses were only partly reachable [D05 caveat]. So every absence claim says "we found none".
  • Our absence claims were tested, and two failed. Norms and regional languages survived two disproof checks each [D05.norms, D05.regional]; "validations outside Bangkok" and "no Thai fluency pass mark" were refuted and reworded [D05.outside_bkk, D05.fluency]. The community-validation, 2009-journal-article and cut-off-by-schooling verdicts had no disproof check [D05.community, D05.t01_abstracts, D05.edu_cutoff].
  • Unverified directions. Carson's 23 and the Parkinson's 14 stay off the ruler [F03.direction, T15.direction, D04.unverified].
  • Two versions of the 2009 Thai validation (60 vs 120 people) disagree [T01]; our icon array uses the meta-analysis's 80% / 80% [D01.inputs].
  • One team, one sample. The 2021 validation and the 2024 analysis use the same 181 people [T03.sample]; the fluency papers use overlapping Chulalongkorn data [T37].
  • Benchmarks. Our only age-specific MCI benchmark is a US guideline, since retired [F17.retired]; our Thai sign that the line sits too high comes from one clinic, whose normal patients had a median of 21.5 [T06.scores]; Thai survey rates depend on the tool, from 3.40% to 92.70% [T30.range]; the national survey found 10.2% impaired with the MMSE-Thai [T44.rate].
  • Our reasoning, not a source. "Internal consistency matters less in a test that mixes abilities on purpose" has no source in our facts.
  • Our arithmetic and readings are labelled "our illustration" on screen [D01–D04].
  • Vendor pages change; we checked them on 7 Nov 2026 [F06 caveat].
  • AI. AI use: we used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, to find and summarise studies, draft our scripts and Q&A answers, and design and code these slides; some background art and textures were generated on our own computer with ComfyUI (FLUX.1 schnell, Z-Image Turbo, and RealVisXL with the MistoLine and xinsir Tile ControlNets). We checked every number against the source we cite: the full paper where we had it, otherwise its abstract.
